## 1. Who here agrees that Edward Norton's The Incredible Hulk was the most genuine and faithful adaptation of the character?

**Score:** 1799
**Body:** **Do you guys agree with me that Edward Norton's version of The Incredible Hulk was the most faithful and accurate live-action adaptation of the character as depicted in the source material?**

**The Hulk in the comics was always meant to be a near-indestructable and unstoppable monster triggered by rage or anxiety. His human form Bruce Banner was written as a deeply vulnerable, repressed and isolated person struggling with severe Dissociative Identity Disorder.**

**I believe Norton perfectly captured Banner's internal turmoil, pain and his struggle to find acceptance with himself as well as his powerful Hulk alter-ego within the narrative of the film.**

## 2. Thoughts on Collateral (2004) by Michael Mann?

**Score:** 829
**Body:** Here are my thoughts:

Flabbergasting cinematography of downtown LA. Besides the astonishingly stunning background of nighttime Los Angeles, the lighting, both in the interior of the car and outside on the streets or in places such as the club are done uncommonly splendidly. The subtle neon lighting focused primarily on Max in the cab, meanwhile Vincent sits in the back in the shadow mirrors the theme of the film with immaculate precision, consolidating the experience. Such use of neon lighting strongly reminds me of the film ‘Drive’, directed by Nicholas Winding Refn, which depicts more or less similar themes. Furthermore, the actual idea of a cab driver held hostage by what initially seemed like a regular passenger for a whole night is, to be fair, unique in itself. Finally, the dialogues were written masterfully. As such, ‘Collateral’, technically speaking, was executed Extremely well. 

Full review on Letterboxd: https://boxd.it/fI9Ouz

## 5. I have given Sinners multiple watchings, and just can't bring myself to see it as the masterpiece people treat it as.

**Score:** 224
**Body:** For starters, let me start off saying I am not claiming it is bad. It was enjoyable enough that I'm not mad I've watched several times since it came out. While I have many complaints, the cinematography is excellent, and the music is great too. I would ultimately give it a 5/10.

For starters, the movie is essentially a From Dusk Till Dawn Ripoff (bad choice of movie to pull from imo). The movie starts as basically a historical southern drama with supernatural implications. And then after like 80 minutes of awful pacing and insufferable dialog the vampires show up and it turns to a siege film.

The issue of the antagonist is a primary criticism. There is no tangible antagonist for the first 2/3rds of the film. There is plenty of conflict but nothing that is presented as urgent like you would expect in a horror movie, considering it was marketed as one. Now, there are no hard and fast rules to any genre, so it's not like you have follow the pack on this. But the audience in this genre is expecting something. It does not make them ask "What terrible thing is going to happen to them?" "What is approaching them?" "How will they get out of this?" The audience is effectively told they need to wait for the horror movie they came for to ever start.

Now, there are actually some solid films in the horror genre that have a slow start. But the difference is, this functions to build dread, and not to world build like in Sinners. Movies like the Shining and the Thing come to mind here. They build a sense of dread with their slow start. Sinners builds the juke joint, the characters, music, period and racial atmosphere. It does not do anything to make itself feel like a horror movie. This means the horror portion doesn't feel any scarier when it finally arrives. It just arrives much later. Being slow isn't a death sentence for movies in general, including horror films. But in this genre you need to utilize it to build suspense. This film sits in an awkward ground where it builds up to a point where the vampires are not shocking, but also not enough to make the beginning of the movie frightening in any way.

The strongest criticism I can make of the horror mechanics themselves, is that once the vampires arrive, they become rapidly legible. The audience and characters quickly learn what they are. They see them. They understand them. They learn the rules. And as a result the threat becomes physical and tactical, rather than scary. In doing this, the movie sacrifices epistemological uncertainty, which is, frankly one of modt useful resources in the entire genre of horror. The level of understanding the writers give the audience and characters can greatly change the atmosphere from unsettling and paranoid to basically just an action film with some supernatural shit.

Despite this disadvantage based on the characters and audience knowledge if the vampires. They could have leveraged it. Think about the Thing. The movie is primarily driven by a sense of paranoia derived from not being able to tell friend from foe. The vampires in Sinners, retain their personality. They have emotionally manipulative skills. They \*\*want\*\* to be invited inside.

Instead of leveraging this to create an atmosphere of "Who can be trusted? Who has been compromised?" the entire movie is essentially at this point in the film boiled down to "keep those motherfucking vampires outside."

If Coogler would have even spent 20 minutes building some mystery on maybe someone being secretly turned and acting from the inside, it could have created drastic changes in how the horror mechanics come across. Now the juke joint is psychologically claustrophobic. But no, there was no thought of such an idea.

The thematic concepts of the movie, which is what I suspect has garnered most of its praise outside of the excellent cinematography and score, is absolutely a strong point of the film. However, the great and thoughtful provoking themes are all in the boring first half of the movie. Things like Christianity can both be oppressive and also foster community. Blues can represent liberation but also temptation. Economic independence can exist alongside criminality. White society is simultaneously economically dependent upon Black culture and violently hostile toward Black autonomy. Well, once the vampire siege starts, this is all thrown out the window. To say what I said earlier, it quickly becomes "keep those motherfucking vampires outside."

The climax of the movie becomes this massive spectacle, becoming excitingly violent and intense, however it does this all without increasing the horror in equal increments. The violence is not one of dread or terror. But one of catharsis.

Think of it like this,

Dread: "Something horrible might happen."

Terror: "Something horrible is happening."

Action: "Kill the thing that's doing the horrible thing."

Obviously in this case, Sinners falls into the last category.

Now to address the elephant in the room, that will probably tilt some readers (oh well). I think horror primarily driven by black identity and this duality of being wanted and hated is powerful, but very overdone at this point. It is simply no longer powerful and the stick is hitting a dead horse. We need black films, and black horror movies. But it doesn't always need to be about black identity. Ever since Get Out (the best of this sub genre of black identity horror) there has been this overly saturated reoccurring theme in horror where blackness is simultaneously desired, consumed, imitated, fetishized, or economically useful by white society while also being feared, excluded, controlled, or hated. That contradivtion is totally real and historically rich enough to sustain some movies. But once enough movies use it as their primary metaphor, you start recognizing the premise bwfore the story has even developed. 

All of these films, whether it is Get Out, Them, Candyman, Bad Hair, Antebellum, etc play into this theme to various degrees. 

Sinners, especially, leans into it. The racism and cultural material is more nuanced than just "racism is the monster." But it still plays with the tired Get Out theme of "acceptance into a dominant white collective at the cost of something essential about yourself and/or your culture." That is what makes the vampires' offer simultaneously attractive and horrifying (or at least what makes it supposed to be horrifying)

The unintended consequence of this? Black characters can start feeling trapped inside allegory. All the while, a white protagonist can fight a demon because there's a fucking demon in his god damn basement. A Black protagonist? He gets a demon that represents racial trauma, and his grandmother's ghost represents inherited memory, and the haunted house represents segregation, and suddenly every black horror movie has to carry a sociology dissertation on its back.

The solution to this isn't less black horror movies. It is to encourage the black filmmaker to make horror movies without black identity being the primary driver of the film. Not every monster needs to stop mid movie and essentially go "I represent the contradictory nature of white America's consumption of Black culture." At some point the monster should just be a fuckin monster. Or it becomes the laughably tired premise that it is today. Out of influx of black made horror films since Get Out, ironically I think Peele's other films Us and Nope are the only ones that don't heavily lean into this as a main thematic element.

I want to note that I don't even blame the directors, the writers or the producers for that. I mostly blame consumers for repeatedly asking for the same shit over and over again and consuming it up with a big smile. It's a great thematic premise but it has lost all entertainment value and I would appreciate seeing something different at this point.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Why do films often make us sympathize with the hedonist rather than the disciplined man?

**Score:** 43
**Body:** I was thinking about *Danton* (1983) and *Amadeus* (1984), and noticed a similarity between the central conflicts.

In *Danton*, you have Danton vs. Robespierre. Danton is excessive, sensual, charismatic, loves food, women, drinking and life in general. Robespierre is almost the opposite: disciplined, controlled, austere, ideological and willing to sacrifice personal pleasure for what he believes is right.

Then in *Amadeus* you get something similar with Mozart and Salieri. Mozart is vulgar, impulsive, childish and hedonistic, while Salieri is disciplined, serious, restrained and has devoted his entire life to music and to God.

Yet in both cases I find myself sympathizing much more with the less disciplined character.

Maybe part of the reason is that discipline can improve what you already have, but it cannot necessarily give you the thing you want most. Salieri can dedicate his entire life to music, but he cannot discipline himself into becoming Mozart. Mozart seems almost "touched by God", which makes Salieri's sacrifices feel tragically useless.

There seems to be something similar going on with Danton. Robespierre can be more disciplined, more morally rigid and more devoted to the Revolution, but he can't simply decide to have Danton's charisma or his connection with ordinary people. Danton walks into a room and people respond to him. Robespierre has to rely much more on ideas, institutions and eventually coercion.

I wonder if that's why cinema often makes the hedonistic character more attractive. They represent something spontaneous and alive that can't be produced through self-control alone: talent, charisma, humor, sensuality, maybe even a kind of grace.

And perhaps there's also something unsettling about extreme discipline itself. Discipline is usually considered a virtue, but once someone starts treating every spontaneous desire as weakness, it can turn into resentment toward people who seem to possess naturally what they had to deny themselves.

Salieri seems like the clearest example: "I did everything right, so why did God give *him* the gift?"

Robespierre's relationship with Danton feels like a political version of the same problem.

Do you think this is a real recurring theme in films? And are there good examples where the opposite happens — where the disciplined, restrained character is clearly the more sympathetic one?

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Because it's a fantasy. Many of us deep down wish we could be hedonistic but the realities of life prevent it. Watching a film about someone like that means we get to share that experience without any of the risk to our health or relationships. I think there often are films about disciplined people, too, although none or springing to mind
  - Not to mention these hedonistic people usually die young, while the boring guy lives to old age.
2. I think you're leaving out a very specific thing in your analysis:

Jealousy.

Jealousy, obsession, and entitlement. Those are ugly things to carry with yourself. Perhaps had someone like Salieri (in the film) devoted his life to himself as opposed to comparing himself to someone he is absolutely not then perhaps his own masterpiece would have came to him. His own expression.
  - To be fair, Mozart exhibits plenty of childish jealousy of the kind that leads him to openly insult colleagues whom he perceives as undeservedly advancing ahead of him. Not as bad as Salieri plotting to destroy a rival’s career and life, obviously.

It’s crucial to the film’s theme that Mozart is not a good man in a conventional, outward sense. A drunk, spendthrift and philander who fritters away his family’s money and cheats on his wife and insults his colleagues both to their faces and behind their backs. And his talent is completely unconnected to this. But Salieri’s pro forma goodness stands revealed as egotistical calculation once he doesn’t get what he considers his just reward, and with little hesitation he plunges headlong into behavior morally worse than Mozart’s by far.

Maybe God saw what was really in Salieri’s heart - ego, hypocrisy - and sent Mozart to reveal to Salieri what he really was.
3. I think this is a fundamental misreading of Amadeus tbh. Mozart’s lifestyle can hardly be considered hedonistic. I think it’s critical to the story being told that Mozart is NOT particularly flawed as a man. He’s childish, sure, in a way that makes Salieri find him annoying to be around, but I really don’t think that’s the same thing. It’s Salieri who makes a pass at Mozart’s wife, and it’s Salieri who sins and feels rage and jealousy. Mozart dies believing that Salieri is his friend who truly wants the best for him. 
  - Also I don't think Salieri is unsympathetic. He's flawed but in a way that makes you feel for him and that many people can relate to.
    - He’s not unsympathetic! He’s the multi-dimensional protagonist of a really great script! But I think it would be odd to frame him as a disciplined and pious figure in contrast to Mozart’s hedonism. Movie character Mozart is hardly living a rockstar lifestyle, and movie character Salieri’s piety is hypocritical and shallow at best, at worst his constant talk of God is the bitter ramblings of a guy who needs to blame SOMETHING for not being as talented as Mozart, because he refuses to accept “you’re just not as talented as Mozart” as a plausible answer.

I say movie character because I’ve heard the story has very little to do with real life, I’m not an expert, I don’t know. Point is, at no point in watching Amadeus multiple times have I ever felt that Salieri’s musings on God were this sincere religious screed of a true believer. 
      - Not to mention the fact that Salieri's life is undoubtedly successful. Salieri is the one with the cushy job and the stable income the constant eating of fancy foods (like sugar!) and the ear of the most powerful men in Europe!
4. Its the classic Apollonian and Dionysian character archetypes. One is enlightened and composed, the other is hedonistic and reckless.

You find the same combination in many stories, another good example is Ripley and Dickey from "Talented mr. Ripley". 

One flew over the cuckoos nest's Randle McMurphy (Nicholson) is also a Dionysian archetype that enters and challenges an entire cast and setting of composed/rule following men (institution).

In my humble opinion, this kind of man is attractive to audiences, mostly males, because he signals freedom from constraints that most people feel every day, fear of judgment, social rules, responsibility etc.

That can be especially compelling to other men because male socialization puts a lot of emphasis on self-control, competence and not appearing "weak". This man signals "none of that owns me" , even when this "irreverent" behavior is destructive eventually.

You see this every day in organized groups (workplace dynamics, friend groups, etc) where people usually pack and leadership is formed, to an extreme extend, this is how the "man-o-sphere" works as well, this is what young men are attracted to when they follow those clowns. 


5. Aren’t Rocky and Pursuit of Happyness movies that make us sympathize with the disciplined man?

By which I mean: just like you can find movies with the “trope” you mention, you can find the opposite. And I’d say my examples are movies that are much more famous than your examples.

## 2. One tragic thing about Hubert in La Haine (1995)

**Score:** 25
**Body:** I believe many pointed out in all the reviews how Hubert was the voice of reason and how he wanted to get away from the ghetto and the violence. However, I want to point out that Hubert wasn’t the voice of reason for the entire movie, and step by step, by the end of the movie, he was kind of a little bit broken emotionally.

In the beginning, Hubert was the voice of reason and tried to convince Vinz not to do it, but as the movie progressed and violence escalated, Hubert got more unhinged too. He was tortured by the police in Paris along with Said, and I think that also took a toll on him. The whole story takes place not long after the Rodney King incident in LA, and they even mentioned it. And by the end of the story, Hubert was tired of Vinz and genuinely tried to push Vinz to shoot the skinhead. Maybe deep down he knew Vinz wouldn’t be able to do it, but still, it was risky.

The thing that gets me the most, although Vinz was angered for most of the movie, Vinz wasn’t as close with Abdel as he was with Hubert and Said, which is part of the reason why he was able to let it go in the end. And Hubert tried to distance himself from the violence as much as he could; he wasn’t going to avenge some dude he barely knew, for some twisted idea of revenge or justice.

And by the end of it, with all the recent events that took a toll on Hubert emotionally, the situation completely unfolded in the opposite direction in the ending.

Now it wasn’t just some dude who got killed, but his close friend. Killed not out of emotion, but out of pure negligence and carelessness. And Hubert knew that if things were let go, the police officer would possibly never receive justified punishment. And here he was, with a loaded gun in his hand. That was the final straw for him. He tried to get away from the violence, but in the end the violence got as close and as personal to him as it possibly could. He snapped, and the question is, who wouldn’t snap being in his shoes?

That’s what gets me the most about this ending. In any other movie, killing a main character right in the end like that would probably leave a bad taste in the mouth of a viewer. It would feel trashy, pointless, and unsatisfying. But here it’s the opposite. The whole movie was about coming to this moment, about this escalation right in the end.

## 4. Thoughts on cinema depictions of the Vietnam War and "historical truth" in fiction

**Score:** 23
**Body:** Someone asked for an example for a movie that sets the record straight on a historical event. I made a comment, but I put so much work in it, it became sort of a little essay. I thought you might be interested in it.

Art is always subjective but for the sake of the argument, let's look at the Vietnam War. Also I competely escalated my bad.

- The Little Girl of Hanoi (1974). A Vietnamese movie about a child that is very good but also unsurprisingly propagandistic as fuck.

- The Deer Hunter (1978). Great film on trauma of war, maybe. Absolutely terrible depiction of the Vietnam War and of Vietnamese, who are just almost just evil in that film lol.

- Apocalypse Now (1979). An outstanding portrayal of war, trauma, madness. A very poor historical depiction of the War. Vietnam is merely a backdrop. The Vietnamese are heavily dehumanized in the film. There are no South Vietnamese comrades, nor any Vietnamese enemy who is anything more than a faceless adversary. Sadly, THE Vietnam War film.

- When the Tenth Month Comes (1984). A Vietnamese movie about a woman who loses her husband in the war. Film about loss, family, grief, not just battles. Fucking awesome movie.

- Platoon (1986). Significantly better. Historically very believable. You notice that the director Oliver Stone experienced the war. Still, however, it's the American story, and Vietnamese are the enemy.

- Full Metal Jacket (1987). Extremely realistic in terms of the grueling first half, but the second half is very stylistic. Vietnamese remain a faceless mass apart from stereotypical depictions of Vietnamese prostitutes. No insights into the Vietnamese, neither allies nor enemies. Once again, US centric. To Kubrick's credit, all his films are sort of explorations of humans capacity for violence and how civilization can control or unleash it... could have worked with realistic Vietnamese tho.

- Hamburger Hill (1987). Fairly realistic, American-centric.

- Good Morning, Vietnam (1987). Most sympathetic depiction of Vietnamese so far, but obviously not at all historically accurate and completely US-centric.

- Born on the 4th of July (1989). Historically pretty accurate, and also very anti-imperialistic. Again, it lacks the Vietnamese perspective though. Mind you, that is not necessarily bad if the film, you know, doesn't depict Vietnamese as like wild non-people like Apocalypse Now did. It's just an unfortunate pattern overall. Good film, just again one-sided.

- Casualties of War (1989). One of the very few, if not only films of that era that actually depicts (a) Vietnamese as victim(s) of American violence. However, it is again told through the experience of American soldiers.

- Heaven and Earth (1993). Again Oliver Stone, who actually depicts the life of a Vietnamese woman. Vietnamese with family, fears, problems, violence from both sides. Oliver Stone is a real one.

- We Were Soldiers (2002). Actually a film that depicts North Vietnamese not just as an unhuman mass. They have family and lives. But of course it's mostly about American soldiers, who are of course extremely brave and heroic. Vietnam did not like that film at all.

- Vietgone (2015). Not a movie, a musical. It does basically what Hamilton sort of tries to do but kind of whitewashes. It tells the immigrant story. The story of Vietnamese refugees. And their lives. It twists this whole classic American perspective, puts it right on its head. Giving the American characters stereotypical ways of talking, one may say, is problematic, which in a vacuum it is. But within context, especially as an American musical, this shit gets the people thinking. It's a mirror. It's fucking awesome. But, of course, it's not "the" truth.

In 2015, the novel The Sympathizer was released, written by Viet Thanh Nguyen. Park Chan-wook, by the way, actually adapted it into a TV show, you know, the director of Oldboy, starring Robert Downey Jr. as every single antagonistic American in that film. Which is a fun little twist, because, you know, that's sort of very much what the Americans did for a long time.

But the show is too meta, the book is much, much, much better. In fact, I'd say it's a modern classic. It's about a North Vietnamese spy and set right after the war. Well, the official ending of the war, but one of the key points of that novel is also that the war didn't really end for the Vietnamese. And this man operates in the USA and Vietnam, has comrades both from the capitalists as well as the communists. And as the title already very well puts, that story is a lot about trying to understand what the fuck this shit was. Honestly, I think it's an absolute must-read in terms of war fiction and American history. It also really fucking hates Apocalypse Now.

If there ever really was a fiction media that set the record straight, it's this. But, say the Oliver Stone films, for example, are fire. The American perspective is also real. The problem is that it dominates the entire narrative. The novel The Sympathizer also puts it rather succinctly, by the way, that this is the first war where the losers write history (globally).

A careful person would now say, you need non-fiction for actual understanding or getting closer to truth, as fiction is always subjective, inherently. Simultaneously, people don't, the vast majority of people do not remember World War II from history books. They remember it from the movies they have seen. The longer back it goes, the more this is so. Most people thinking of the Nazi era don't remember the Shoah documentary (watch it!!!) or EVEN a school trip to a KZ - they remember Schindler's List.

Which makes this an interesting topic. At the end of the day, there is not really one fiction that sets the record straight. You don't need to set the record straight for Oliver Stone's Platoon. It is a legitimate story, but it is the American perspective. You don't need to set the record straight on When the Tenth Month Comes, which is in and of itself incredibly accurate, but it is also the Vietnamese perspective. It's a jigsaw puzzle, and fiction can be incredibly helpful to understand the picture. But it will never be the whole truth. An emotional truth, perhaps a cultural one - but not true objectivity. In fact, even documentaries and the most carefully written history book is never simply "the" truth. But non-fiction of course is a necessary fundament to actually understand. To know. Fiction is valuable and can be much more than entertainment - it helps to grasp. And it is not simply less than non-fiction per se. But you need non-fiction as a roadmap. Fiction cannot be a roadmap; it is always a portrait.

## 5. Indian adaptations of Danish comedies

**Score:** 15
**Body:** I recently noticed that the Danish SORTE KUGLER (2009) had been adapted into the Indian THANK GOD (2022). It had been a good while since I watched it, so I made it a double feature.

SORTE KUGLER is a sort of modern take on A CHRISTMAS CAROL. A thoroughly unpleasant real estate agent is involved in a car crash and ends up in an heavenly game show, where he must demonstrate that he can behave like a decent human being, or else. So it's the classic formula of enjoying the antics of a problematic character followed by some sort of moralistic wrap-up to justify it. Only, this one seems a bit more raw, a bit more honest, a little like it actually mean it.

Anders Matthesen, who wrote, directed, and played the lead in SORTE KUGLER, is an edgy and provocative comedian, but what sets him apart from other edgy and provocative comedians is his humane honesty. It's provocative, sure, but not just that. When he aim to portray an unpleasant real estate agent, the result is a powerhouse of bitterness and bile. THANK GOD, by contrast, goes for less distasteful character, played by one Sidharth Malhotra who I assume had to be shown as a fundamentally charming dude. Which sort of grinds against him supposedly being a bad person with an redemption arc.

While THANK GOD talks about karma and mention the English truism "what comes around goes around" (The english title of SORTE KUGLER just happens to be WHAT GOES AROUND), even with this focus, it chickens out of the ending of the Danish version. But that's not too bad. It is, after all, another movie. Even if THANK GOD basically follow the same story, it has been given the full Bollywood treatment with lavish music numbers and over-the-top sugarcoated feel-good energy, and admittedly much grander production value. Where the game show is kept in green-toned white in SORTE KUGLER, the one in THANK GOD is a lush grandiouse CGI setpiece.

Rewatching SORTE KUGLER right after THANK GOD felt like being thrown straight into cold water. That house sale opening really sets the scene, while also getting the exposition out of the way.

SORTE KUGLER is the better film. Snappier, more focused. But I found THANK GOD to be an enjoyable ride on its own, if one can tolerate the low-stake blatant feel-good overload. It was fun to see how the same story is being delivered in India versus Denmark. Especially since the adaptation follow its source pretty closely. The game show trials the protagonist are subjected to are kept relatively intact in the remake. While the lust trial obviously is just an excuse for a grand musical number (and I'll go on record and say I aprove!) there were also some depth. I really liked the repeated-joke lesson.

Both movies does well on the music front, with THANK GOD bombastic score contrasting wildly with the more somber tone of the Danish one. SORTE KUGLER features 8 Danish songs, among them "Kom Igen" by Kim Larsen, the eighties hit "Video Video" (the only upbeat of the bunch) and "Hun Er Fri" by Tue West, a musician frequently mentioned in the movie.
